title: Nearly 70% of Diet and Exercise Videos Are Misleading
paragraphs: Many people look for advice about healthy eating and exercise on social media. However, a new study from Australia suggests that most of this advice may not be accurate.

The study was carried out by researchers at Flinders University in Adelaide and published in the Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science in 2026. The researchers searched TikTok and Instagram using three popular hashtags: #healthylifestyle, #nutrition and #cleaneating. They then looked closely at 300 videos, 150 from each platform. The study focused on content aimed at women or featuring women. The videos were collected in May 2025, and they were about 26 seconds long on average.
The researchers found that 68% of the information about diet and exercise in the videos was misleading or deceptive.

They also checked whether the people who made the videos had any qualifications in nutrition or health. About 78% of the videos were made by influencers without qualifications. The results showed a big difference between the two groups. About 75% of the content made by unqualified influencers was misleading, compared with about 41% of the content made by qualified people. Only 4.7% of the content made by unqualified influencers was accurate.

Many videos also focused on people's bodies. For example, lean, muscular bodies appeared in about 71% of the Instagram videos and 47% of the TikTok videos. In addition, nearly one in three videos gave strict food rules, and about 20% suggested that a person's food choices showed their value as a person. About 10% of the videos showed people exercising too much or exercising to make up for eating.
The researchers are worried that this kind of content could encourage an unhealthy obsession with eating "clean" food.
However, the study only looked at the videos themselves. It did not measure how they affect the people who watch them.
